stories.title: Will Johor Bahru Be Easy to Walk Around When the RTS Link Opens?
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's new train link to Johor Bahru is almost ready, but the city on the other side is built for cars, not walkers!
summary: The RTS Link is a new train that will connect Woodlands in Singapore to Bukit Chagar in Johor Bahru (JB), Malaysia. It is meant to make crossing over much faster - turning a car journey that can take over an hour with traffic jams into just a few minutes on the train.

But there is a problem. Once you step off the train in JB, the city centre is not easy to walk around. It was built mainly for cars, with wide roads, few proper pavements, and hardly any covered walkways linking places together.

Transport experts say this could be a big issue. If people cannot easily walk to shops, offices or attractions after leaving the station, it defeats the purpose of having a fast train in the first place.

Malaysian authorities are now talking to experts, including a famous international design company called Zaha Hadid Architects, to find ways to make JB's city centre more 'walkable' - meaning safer, nicer and easier to explore on foot.

lenses.me: If your family plans a day trip to JB on the new train, you might still need to grab a taxi or ride-hailing car once you arrive, since walking around may not be easy yet.
lenses.family: Families who often cross the Causeway for shopping or food may find the train ride quick, but still need to plan how to get around once they land in JB.
lenses.friends: Your friends who talk about weekend trips to JB might start comparing notes on the best ways to get around town.
lenses.nation: Singapore has spent a lot of money building the RTS Link, so how well it works on the JB side also affects whether Singaporeans will actually use it.
lenses.world: This story shows a lesson many cities around the world face: building a fast train is not enough if the streets around it are not designed for people to walk safely.

stories.title: Singapore's Senior Minister Flies to Two Countries You May Not Know
stories.headline_kid: Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong is visiting Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to make new friends for Singapore!
summary: Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong is Singapore's former Prime Minister. He often travels overseas to meet leaders of other countries and build friendships for Singapore.

From 24 to 31 August, he is visiting two countries in Central Asia called Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. These countries are far from Singapore, located between Europe and China, and are known for having lots of natural resources like oil, gas and minerals.

During the trip, SM Lee will meet the presidents and prime ministers of both countries. These meetings help Singapore build stronger friendships and business links with countries that many Singaporeans may not have visited or heard much about before.
Even though these countries seem far away and unfamiliar, good relationships with them can help Singapore trade more goods, attract more investment, and make more friends around the world.

lenses.me: You might not have heard of Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan before - this is a great chance to find them on a map!
lenses.family: Your family might one day buy products connected to these countries because of stronger trade ties, like cotton or oil-related goods.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can challenge each other to find these countries on a globe or atlas.
lenses.nation: Singapore is a small country, so making friends with many nations around the world helps us trade and stay connected globally.
lenses.world: This visit is part of how countries build friendships and do business together, even when they are very far apart.

stories.title: Cargo Ship Heading to Singapore Sinks Near India
stories.headline_kid: A big cargo ship on its way to Singapore sank near India, and rescuers are searching for missing crew members.
summary: A large cargo ship called the MV Ocean Winner sank off the eastern coast of India on Sunday. The ship was sailing from Paradip Port in India, and its next stop was supposed to be Singapore.

Ships like this one, called bulk carriers, carry huge amounts of raw materials such as coal, grain or metal ores across the sea. Singapore's port is one of the busiest in the world, so many such ships pass through or head to us every day.
Sadly, 22 crew members went missing when the ship sank. So far, only two people have been rescued. The Indian navy is racing to search the waters to find the rest.

This incident reminds us how important - and sometimes risky - sea travel is for bringing goods to countries like Singapore. It also shows how rescue teams work hard to save sailors even far out at sea.

lenses.me: Many things you use every day - like the paper in your books or the metal in your bicycle - may have travelled to Singapore on ships just like this one.
lenses.family: Your family might buy products that arrived in Singapore by cargo ship, showing how connected we are to the sea.
lenses.friends: You can talk to your friends about how goods travel from other countries to Singapore by sea.
lenses.nation: Singapore's port relies on ships from many countries, so safety at sea matters a lot to us.
lenses.world: This tragedy is a reminder that international rescue efforts are important when disasters happen far out at sea.

stories.title: More Ads in Singapore Are Made by AI—But Some Could Backfire
stories.headline_kid: Computers can now create adverts in seconds, but experts warn that badly made ones could make companies look silly.
summary: More companies in Singapore are now using generative AI - smart computer programmes that can create pictures, videos and words - to make their advertisements. Think of it like a robot artist that can draw a poster or film a short video just from a written description, in minutes instead of days.

Businesses like this because it is much faster and cheaper than hiring photographers, actors or designers for every advert. Creative agencies in Singapore say more companies have been asking for AI-made adverts over the past six months.

But experts are warning that not all AI-made ads are good quality. Some can look strange, unrealistic, or even confusing - like a person with six fingers or words that don't make sense. If a brand posts a bad AI advert, customers might trust that brand less.
So while AI can help make advertising faster, companies still need to check their ads carefully before showing them to the public, to make sure they still look professional and trustworthy.

lenses.me: The next time you see a strange or slightly odd-looking advert online, it might have been made by AI!
lenses.family: Your parents might notice more AI-made ads while shopping online or watching videos.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can try spotting AI-made pictures or videos - look for small mistakes like odd hands or blurry backgrounds.
lenses.nation: Singapore's advertising and marketing industry is changing quickly because of AI, and companies need to adapt carefully.
lenses.world: This is part of a bigger global trend of businesses using AI tools to save time and money.

compo_words.example: The software can generate a short advertisement within minutes.

stories.title: Can Singapore Football Keep This Exciting Momentum Going?
stories.headline_kid: After an exciting run in the ASEAN Championship, people are asking: how much should Singapore care about football?
summary: Singapore's national football team, known as the Lions, has recently played exciting matches in the ASEAN Championship, including a match against Thailand at the huge Rajamangala Stadium. Many fans travelled to cheer them on, creating a real buzz around the team.

This is a big change. For a while, interest in local football had been 'gasping for air' - meaning it was struggling and not many people were excited about it. Now, thanks to good performances, more Singaporeans are talking about and supporting the Lions again.

A sports commentator says this is a good moment for Singapore to think about how much support - like funding, facilities and encouragement - should be given to football here, so this new excitement doesn't fade away.

The idea is simple: when a team does well, more people want to watch and support it. But keeping that excitement going long-term takes more effort, like training young players and building better facilities.

lenses.family: Your family might enjoy watching a Lions match together on TV or even at the stadium.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can chat about your favourite Lions players and matches.
lenses.nation: Singapore is deciding how much to invest in football to keep this excitement alive for years to come.
lenses.world: This shows how sport can unite a country and bring people together, even in a small nation like Singapore.
